title: January minutes expose a disagreement about how restrictive policy already was
summary: The minutes released on 18 February explain the 27–28 January decision to hold at 3.50–3.75%. After 75 basis points of cuts the previous year, supporters of the hold generally saw the rate as within the range of plausible neutral estimates. The two participants favouring a cut regarded it as materially restrictive and gave greater weight to employment risks. Stephen Miran and Christopher Waller cast the formal votes for a quarter-point reduction. The disagreement concerned the degree of restraint already being applied, not simply the preferred speed of movement towards a neutral rate everyone agreed on.

The employment evidence made the distinction important. December unemployment was 4.4%, unchanged from September. Average fourth-quarter payroll growth was negative, but the October end of a federal deferred resignation programme accounted for a large government payroll decline. Average additions in November and December were comparable with the third-quarter pace. Almost all participants saw both layoffs and hiring as low. That combination can stabilise unemployment while leaving a fragile market for new jobseekers. A modest decline in hiring or a rise in layoffs could matter disproportionately when finding another job is already difficult. Some participants also cited lower immigration as a reason that weak payroll gains need not indicate a large demand shortfall.

Inflation showed opposing movements beneath a similar aggregate reading. November headline and core PCE inflation were both 2.8%. Core goods inflation strengthened, which staff largely attributed to tariffs, while housing services contributed to slower services inflation. Staff estimated December headline and core PCE inflation at 2.9% and 3.0% and flagged shutdown-related data collection problems that had probably depressed measured price levels. Those were estimates at the meeting. The uncertainty qualified any inference from a small month-to-month change. Many officials expected tariff effects to fade, but business contacts also reported plans to pass costs through. Most participants saw a meaningful risk of inflation remaining above 2%.

The staff raised its activity projection and expected growth to exceed potential through 2028, helped by financial conditions and fiscal policy. That was a conditional staff forecast. Participants differed on the policy it would take to secure disinflation. Several saw room for further cuts if prices followed their expected path. Some wanted an extended hold, and several would have supported language allowing increases should inflation persist. The two formal dissents therefore understate the breadth of views on future policy. A preference for retaining the option of a hike was distinct from voting to hike in January.

The market report helps distinguish the levels already priced before the meeting. Market indicators pointed to one or two quarter-point cuts during 2026, while the median of respondents' most likely paths in the Desk survey indicated two. A slight Treasury-curve steepening largely reflected longer yields rising a few basis points with short yields little changed. In mortgages, the manager linked a narrowing against Treasuries to news about possible agency portfolio expansion, but judged a large refinancing wave unlikely because prevailing rates exceeded average rates on mortgages outstanding. Those observations describe the period before the deliberations. They are not returns around the public release of these minutes.

The implementation discussion added a separate funding-market signal. The effective funds rate sat just below interest on reserves, and year-end repo pressure was milder than anticipated. Contacts cited reserve-management purchases, Treasury cash balances, revisions to standing repo operations and advance funding preparations. The manager projected reserves around $3 trillion for much of the forecast period, with a tax-related decline in April. The record treats these as operational conditions and projections. Equating purchases for reserve management with a change in the Committee's chosen policy rate would obscure the distinction the January decision maintained.

questions.question: Could the neutral-rate disagreement be tested against actual borrowing conditions?
questions.detail: Reconstruct real short rates using several contemporaneous expectations measures and examine loan terms across households and businesses. Differentiate changes in benchmark rates from changes in credit spreads and access. Continued tight credit among small borrowers can coexist with accommodative funding for large issuers, making an aggregate neutral-rate inference difficult.

questions.question: Was low hiring a stable response to labour supply or a vulnerability to rising unemployment?
questions.detail: Compare hiring, layoffs, job finding, participation and the distribution of payroll gains after adjusting for the federal payroll event. Keep the evidence policymakers had in January separate from later revisions. A rise in separations with weak job finding would put more weight on the minority's downside scenario.

questions.question: What additional information did investors receive on 18 February?
questions.detail: Compare expectations immediately before and after publication with the January statement and subsequent public communication. Test whether later contracts or option-implied upside risks moved more than the front contract as investors learned about support for two-sided guidance. Keep the intermeeting market changes described by the Desk out of the release-event window.
